headline: Bronte Capital uses AMP's 40-year decline as a cautionary tale of management failure through short-term incentive misalignment destroying a once-dominant Australian financial institution
reasoning: AMP was one of five pillars of the Australian financial system in the mid-1980s, with a captive tied-planner network that dominated the Australian savings market. Open-architecture competitors (e.g. MLC) began winning share because they offered a wider product menu; this continued for four decades. AMP management knew that opening up its network was the right strategic response but refused to do so because it would have halved profits in the short term. No CEO was willing to take that pain, so the decision was deferred until AMP became irrelevant. Bronte Capital draws the explicit contrast between AMP's passive decline and Google's proactive pivot into AI, using AMP as the archetypal case of bad short-term incentives producing atrocious long-term outcomes.
quote: AMP management knew that this was coming — and that the right thing to do was to open up the AMP network. But the moment they did so, 30-50% of the money would leave to other providers. No AMP CEO wanted to make the decision that would halve profits so they all deferred the decision. For 40 years. Until they were irrelevant. Bad short-term incentives led to atrocious long-term outcomes. Google faces a similar threat — but its management is superior to AMP's.
